column1:
Cells, ranges and cell references

How does Excel name one box on the sheet, and how do you point to a whole block of boxes in a formula?

A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
B1: =SUM(A1:A3)
column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
A cell is one box on the sheet, and a range is a block of cells.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
सेल = शीट का एक खाना; रेंज = कई खानों का समूह

CODE:
A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
B1: =SUM(A1:A3)

OUTPUT:
60

EXPLANATION:
A cell address is the column letter followed by the row number. A range uses a colon between its first and last cell, so A1:A3 means A1, A2 and A3. Formulas use these addresses so the answer updates when the numbers change.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
Har khane ka ek address hota hai, jaise A1. Kai khane ek saath lene hon to colon lagate hain, jaise A1:A3. Formula me address likhne se number badalne par answer khud badal jata hai.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like a cinema seat number: row and seat together tell you exactly one seat, and a seat block is a group of neighbouring seats.

SYNTAX PATTERN:
=FUNCTION(first_cell:last_cell)

ANATOMY:
A = column letter | 1 = row number | A1 = one cell | A1:A3 = range from A1 down to A3

EXAMPLE 1:
A1: 10
B1: =A1 (shows 10, B1 just points to one cell)

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
B1: =SUM(A1:A3) (shows 60, a range down one column)

EXAMPLE 3:
A1: 5
A2: 10
B1: 15
B2: 20
C1: =SUM(A1:B2) (shows 50, a block across two columns)

VARIATION:
=SUM(A1,A3) adds only A1 and A3 (comma picks separate cells)
=SUM(A:A) adds the whole column A
Name Box: type D10 and press Enter to jump to D10

USED WITH:
SUM, AVERAGE, Name Box, formulas

RELATED CONCEPTS:
Worksheet, Workbook, Named range, Table

ALTERNATIVES:
Named range, Excel Table column reference

FAMILY / GROUP:
cell, range, row, column, address, selection

WHERE IT IS USED:
Budgets and totals | Marks sheets | Any formula you write

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: My total shows 0, what did I do wrong? | B: Check your range; you may have typed A1:A2 instead of A1:A3 and missed a row.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ A1:A3 means only the two cells A1 and A3 → ✓ A1:A3 means every cell from A1 through A3, including A2

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
A1:A3 vs A1,A3: the colon takes the whole block, the comma takes only the cells you name.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not type numbers into a formula when the cell address can be used, or the answer will not update.

WRONG CODE:
A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
B1: =SUM(A1,A3)

RIGHT CODE:
A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
B1: =SUM(A1:A3)

MEMORY TRICK:
Colon = continues through all cells; comma = counts only the ones named.

REAL LIFE: PROJECT / WORK:
A school clerk sums the marks of one student by pointing a formula at the row range of that student.

REAL LIFE: INTERVIEW / EXAM:
Interview question: What is the difference between a cell reference and a range, and which symbol makes a range?

REAL LIFE: DAILY LIFE:
It is like telling a friend your flat number instead of saying the whole street, and a floor range instead of one flat.

column1:
Data types: text, number, date

Why can a cell that looks like a number refuse to add up, and what does Excel secretly store behind a date?

A1: 100
A2: '100 (typed with an apostrophe, so it is text)
B1: =ISNUMBER(A1)
B2: =ISNUMBER(A2)
column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
Excel stores each entry as text, a number or a date, and treats them differently.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
टेक्स्ट = शब्द, नंबर = संख्या, डेट = तारीख

CODE:
A1: 100
A2: '100 (typed with an apostrophe, so it is text)
B1: =ISNUMBER(A1)
B2: =ISNUMBER(A2)

OUTPUT:
B1 shows TRUE and B2 shows FALSE

EXPLANATION:
ISNUMBER checks if a cell holds a real number. A1 is a number, but A2 was stored as text because of the apostrophe, even though it looks the same. Dates are numbers too: Excel counts days from 1 January 1900, and 1 January 2024 is stored as 45292.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
Excel teen cheez alag rakhta hai: text, number aur date. Text ke andar 100 likha ho to wo jodne me nahi aata. Date asal me ek number hai jo din ginta hai.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like a bank counter with separate windows for cash, cheques and letters, each handled by different rules.

SYNTAX PATTERN:
=ISNUMBER(cell) | =ISTEXT(cell)

ANATOMY:
ISNUMBER = test function | cell = what to check | result = TRUE or FALSE

EXAMPLE 1:
A1: Asha
B1: =ISTEXT(A1) (shows TRUE, a word is text)

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: 100
A2: '100
B1: =SUM(A1:A2) (shows 100, SUM skips the text one)

EXAMPLE 3:
A1: =DATE(2024,1,1)
A2: =DATE(2024,3,1)
B1: =A2-A1 (cell format General, shows 60 days)

VARIATION:
Format cell as General to see the date serial number, for example 45292
=VALUE(A2) converts text like "100" into the number 100
Data tab > Text to Columns > Finish converts a column of text numbers

USED WITH:
ISNUMBER, ISTEXT, VALUE, Format Cells

RELATED CONCEPTS:
Number format, Text to Columns, Date serial number, VALUE

ALTERNATIVES:
VALUE function, Text to Columns, multiply by 1

FAMILY / GROUP:
text, number, date, time, logical, error value

WHERE IT IS USED:
Importing data from other systems | Cleaning mark lists | Date calculations like due dates

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: My SUM ignores some numbers in the column, why? | B: They are probably stored as text; look for left-aligned values and convert them.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ Anything that looks like a number is a number → ✓ A value can look like 100 but be stored as text, and then SUM ignores it

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
Text 100 vs number 100: text looks the same but is ignored by SUM and sorts like a word.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not type numbers with extra spaces or apostrophes if you need to calculate with them.

WRONG CODE:
A1: 100
A2: '100
A3: 50
B1: =SUM(A1:A3) (expecting 250)

RIGHT CODE:
A1: 100
A2: '100
A3: 50
B2: =VALUE(A2)
B1: =SUM(A1,B2,A3) (shows 250)

MEMORY TRICK:
Left = Letters (text), Right = Right numbers; this is the default alignment.

REAL LIFE: PROJECT / WORK:
A sales analyst imports a CSV and converts text numbers so that totals match the source report.

REAL LIFE: INTERVIEW / EXAM:
Interview question: Why does SUM give the wrong total when some numbers are stored as text?

REAL LIFE: DAILY LIFE:
It is like a shopkeeper who counts only real notes and puts photocopies of notes aside.

column1:
AutoFill and the fill handle

Which tiny square at a cell's corner lets you drag a pattern or formula down a column?

A1: 1
A2: 2
Select A1:A2, drag the fill handle down to A5
column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
AutoFill copies or continues a pattern by dragging the fill handle.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
ऑटोफ़िल = खींचकर पैटर्न या फ़ॉर्मूला अपने आप भरना

CODE:
A1: 1
A2: 2
Select A1:A2, drag the fill handle down to A5

OUTPUT:
A3 shows 3, A4 shows 4, A5 shows 5

EXPLANATION:
Excel reads the first two values to find the step, here +1, and continues it. For text such as day names it continues the built-in list. For formulas it copies the formula and moves the relative references.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
Do cell select karke handle kheenchoge to Excel pattern samajh kar aage bhar deta hai. Ek hi number ho to wo copy ho jata hai. Formula ho to wo bhi neeche copy hota hai.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like showing a child 2, 4 and then saying carry on; the child continues 6, 8, 10 by the same rule.

SYNTAX PATTERN:
Select cells > drag the fill handle (bottom-right square)

ANATOMY:
Selected cells = the pattern | fill handle = small square | drag direction = where the pattern continues

EXAMPLE 1:
A1: 1
A2: 2
Select A1:A2, drag the handle to A5 (A5 shows 5, a number series)

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: Mon
Drag the handle down to A3 (A2 shows Tue, A3 shows Wed, a text list)

EXAMPLE 3:
A1: 5
A2: 7
A3: 9
B1: =A1*2
Double-click the handle of B1 (B2 shows 14, B3 shows 18, a formula copy)

VARIATION:
A single number such as 5 is copied, not counted, when you drag
Hold Ctrl while dragging a single number to make it count up (Windows)
Click the small Auto Fill Options button after dragging to choose Copy Cells or Fill Series

USED WITH:
Fill series, relative references, Flash Fill, Ctrl+D

RELATED CONCEPTS:
Relative reference, Custom lists, Ctrl+D, Flash Fill

ALTERNATIVES:
Ctrl+D to fill down, Home tab > Fill > Series

FAMILY / GROUP:
AutoFill, fill handle, fill series, fill down, fill right, series

WHERE IT IS USED:
Serial numbers on a list | Dates and months across columns | Copying one formula to every row

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: I typed 1 and dragged but I got 1, 1, 1; why? | B: A single number is copied, so enter 1 and 2 first and drag both cells.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ Dragging one number always counts up, 1, 2, 3 → ✓ A single number is copied; give two cells to show the step, or hold Ctrl while dragging

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
Fill handle vs Ctrl+D: the handle drags to any distance and pattern, Ctrl+D copies the cell above into the selected cells.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not drag blindly over a long list when double-clicking the fill handle does the work in one move.

WRONG CODE:
A1: 1
Drag the handle down to A5 (expecting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

RIGHT CODE:
A1: 1
A2: 2
Select A1:A2 and drag the handle down to A5

MEMORY TRICK:
Two cells show the step; one cell shows only copy.

REAL LIFE: PROJECT / WORK:
An office assistant numbers 200 employee rows by dragging the handle instead of typing every number.

REAL LIFE: INTERVIEW / EXAM:
Interview question: How do you quickly copy a formula down 500 rows without dragging?

REAL LIFE: DAILY LIFE:
It is like a teacher writing the first two roll numbers and asking the class monitor to continue the list.

column1:
Flash Fill

Which feature watches one example you type and then completes the whole column without a formula?

A1: Asha Rao
A2: Sita Devi
B1: Asha (typed by you)
Click B2, press Ctrl+E
column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
Flash Fill copies a pattern you typed once to the other rows.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
फ़्लैश फ़िल = एक उदाहरण देखकर बाकी पंक्तियाँ अपने आप भरना

CODE:
A1: Asha Rao
A2: Sita Devi
B1: Asha (typed by you)
Click B2, press Ctrl+E

OUTPUT:
B2 shows Sita

EXPLANATION:
Excel compares your typed example with the cell beside it and finds the pattern, here the first word. It then fills the rest of the column using that pattern. The result is plain text, not a formula, so it will not update later.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
Pehli row me jo chahiye wo khud likho, phir Ctrl+E dabao. Excel pattern pehchan kar baaki sab bhar deta hai. Ye formula nahi hai, sirf text hai.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like showing a tailor one sample shirt, then asking him to stitch the rest in exactly the same style.

SYNTAX PATTERN:
Type first example > Ctrl+E (or Data tab > Flash Fill)

ANATOMY:
Source column = the data | typed example = the pattern | Ctrl+E = apply to all rows

EXAMPLE 1:
A1: Asha Rao
A2: Sita Devi
B1: Asha
Click B2, press Ctrl+E (B2 shows Sita, a split)

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: Asha
B1: Rao
C1: Asha Rao (typed)
Click C2, press Ctrl+E (joins first and last name for each row)

EXAMPLE 3:
A1: 9876543210
B1: 98765-43210 (typed)
Click B2, press Ctrl+E (adds a dash in the same place for all rows)

VARIATION:
Data tab > Flash Fill does the same as Ctrl+E
File > Options > Advanced > Automatically Flash Fill turns the live suggestion on or off
If the grey preview appears while you type, press Enter to accept it

USED WITH:
Text to Columns, LEFT, MID, CONCAT

RELATED CONCEPTS:
Text to Columns, LEFT and RIGHT, TEXTJOIN, AutoFill

ALTERNATIVES:
Text to Columns, LEFT/MID/RIGHT formulas, TEXTSPLIT in Microsoft 365

FAMILY / GROUP:
Flash Fill, pattern, split, join, extract, clean

WHERE IT IS USED:
Splitting full names | Fixing phone number format | Making email IDs from names

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: I have full names in one column, can I get only first names fast? | B: Type the first name once next to it and press Ctrl+E.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ Flash Fill creates a formula that updates when the data changes → ✓ Flash Fill writes fixed values, so you must run it again after the source changes

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
Flash Fill vs AutoFill: Flash Fill learns a text pattern from an example, while AutoFill continues a number or list series.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not trust Flash Fill blindly on messy data; always scan the results for wrong rows.

WRONG CODE:
A1: Asha Rao
A2: Sita Devi
Select B2 and press Ctrl+E with B1 left empty

RIGHT CODE:
A1: Asha Rao
A2: Sita Devi
B1: Asha (typed)
Click B2, press Ctrl+E

MEMORY TRICK:
Type one, press Ctrl+E, check all.

REAL LIFE: PROJECT / WORK:
A data entry person splits 1,000 full names into first and last name columns in a few seconds.

REAL LIFE: INTERVIEW / EXAM:
Interview question: How can you split a name column without writing a formula?

REAL LIFE: DAILY LIFE:
It is like showing a friend one correctly written address label and asking him to copy the style on the rest.

column1:
Relative vs absolute references ($)

Why does a copied formula sometimes point to the wrong cell, and what sign pins a cell in place?

A2: 200
A3: 300
B1: 0.1 (rate)
C2: =A2*$B$1
C3: =A3*$B$1
column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
A relative reference moves when copied; an absolute reference with dollar signs stays fixed.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
रिलेटिव = कॉपी करने पर बदलता है; एब्सोल्यूट ($) = जगह पर टिका रहता है

CODE:
A2: 200
A3: 300
B1: 0.1 (rate)
C2: =A2*$B$1
C3: =A3*$B$1

OUTPUT:
C2 shows 20 and C3 shows 30

EXPLANATION:
When C2 is copied down, A2 becomes A3 because it is relative. $B$1 stays B1 because both its column and row are locked. This lets every row use the same rate cell.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
Normal reference formula ke saath neeche khisakta hai. Dollar lagane se wo cell wahi rukta hai. Isliye rate wale cell par $ lagate hain.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like asking each student to check the person next to them (relative), but also asking everyone to look at one fixed notice board (absolute).

SYNTAX PATTERN:
A1 (relative) | $A$1 (absolute) | A$1 or $A1 (mixed)

ANATOMY:
$ before the letter = lock the column | $ before the number = lock the row | no $ = free to move

EXAMPLE 1:
A2: 200
A3: 300
C2: =A2*2 (copied to C3 it becomes =A3*2 and shows 600, relative)

EXAMPLE 2:
A2: 200
A3: 300
B1: 0.1
C2: =A2*$B$1 (copied to C3 it stays $B$1 and shows 30, absolute)

EXAMPLE 3:
A2: 2
A3: 3
B1: 4
C1: 5
B2: =$A2*B$1 (shows 8; copied to C3 it becomes =$A3*C$1 and shows 15, mixed)

VARIATION:
F4 once makes $A$1, twice makes A$1, three times makes $A1, four times gives A1 again
Named range, for example Rate, works like an absolute reference
Copying a formula right changes the column letter; copying down changes the row number

USED WITH:
AutoFill, SUM, VLOOKUP, percentage calculations

RELATED CONCEPTS:
AutoFill, Named range, Mixed reference, F4 key

ALTERNATIVES:
Named range, Excel Table structured references

FAMILY / GROUP:
relative, absolute, mixed, anchor, lock, F4

WHERE IT IS USED:
Applying one tax or discount rate to a price list | Multiplication tables | Lookup tables that must not shift

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: Only my first row is right after I drag the formula down; the rest show zero. | B: Your rate cell moved; press F4 to lock it as $B$1.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ A copied formula always points to the same cells as the original → ✓ A normal reference shifts when copied; only the ones with $ stay fixed

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
B1 vs $B$1: B1 shifts when copied, $B$1 never shifts.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not copy a formula that uses a fixed rate cell without first adding the dollar signs.

WRONG CODE:
B1: 10
A2: 200
A3: 300
C2: =A2*B1
C3 (copied) becomes =A3*B2 and shows 0

RIGHT CODE:
B1: 10
A2: 200
A3: 300
C2: =A2*$B$1
C3 (copied) stays =A3*$B$1 and shows 3000

MEMORY TRICK:
Dollar = Done moving; no dollar means the cell can wander.

REAL LIFE: PROJECT / WORK:
A finance analyst applies one GST rate cell to hundreds of price rows using $ in the formula.

REAL LIFE: INTERVIEW / EXAM:
Interview question: What does $A$1 mean, and when would you use it instead of A1?

REAL LIFE: DAILY LIFE:
It is like fixing one price tag to a shelf so that it does not move while the other items change places.

column1:
SUM and AutoSum

Which function adds a block of numbers, and what shortcut types it for you?

A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
A4: =SUM(A1:A3)
column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
SUM adds all the numbers in the cells you give it.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
SUM = जोड़ना, सारी संख्याओं का कुल

CODE:
A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
A4: =SUM(A1:A3)

OUTPUT:
60

EXPLANATION:
SUM adds every number in the range. It ignores text and empty cells in the range. AutoSum, on the Home tab or with Alt+=, writes the SUM formula and guesses the range for you.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
SUM sab number jod deta hai. Text ya khali cell ho to use chhod deta hai. Alt+= dabane se Excel khud formula likh deta hai.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like emptying all small piles of money on a table into one big pile and counting that pile.

SYNTAX PATTERN:
=SUM(number1, [number2], ...)

ANATOMY:
= starts a formula | SUM = function name | ( ) = brackets | A1:A3 = numbers to add

EXAMPLE 1:
A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
A4: =SUM(A1:A3) (shows 60, a simple range)

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
B1: =SUM(A1:A3,5) (shows 65, a range plus a typed number)

EXAMPLE 3:
A1: 10
A2: n/a
A3: 30
B1: =SUM(A1:A3) (shows 40, the text n/a is ignored)

VARIATION:
=SUM(A:A) adds the whole column A
Select A4 under the numbers and press Alt+= then Enter (Windows) for AutoSum
Home tab > Editing group > AutoSum button (the sigma sign) does the same

USED WITH:
AVERAGE, SUMIF, AutoSum, Alt+=

RELATED CONCEPTS:
SUMIF, SUMIFS, AVERAGE, COUNT

ALTERNATIVES:
Plus signs like =A1+A2+A3, the status bar total, SUMIF for conditions

FAMILY / GROUP:
SUM, SUMIF, SUMIFS, SUMPRODUCT, SUBTOTAL, AutoSum

WHERE IT IS USED:
Monthly expense totals | Marks totals | Sales reports

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: How do I add the whole column quickly? | B: Click the empty cell below it and press Alt+=, then Enter.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ SUM will turn text like "five" into 5 → ✓ SUM ignores text in a range, so type real numbers

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
SUM vs SUBTOTAL: SUM adds everything in the range, while SUBTOTAL can skip rows hidden by a filter.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not add a long column with plus signs when one SUM range can do it.

WRONG CODE:
A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
A4: SUM(A1:A3)

RIGHT CODE:
A1: 10
A2: 20
A3: 30
A4: =SUM(A1:A3)

MEMORY TRICK:
SUM = Stack Up Many numbers.

REAL LIFE: PROJECT / WORK:
An accounts assistant totals daily sales in a month column with one SUM formula.

REAL LIFE: INTERVIEW / EXAM:
Interview question: How do you add a column of numbers quickly, and what does SUM do with text?

REAL LIFE: DAILY LIFE:
It is like adding up all the bills on a monthly grocery list.

column1:
AVERAGE, MIN and MAX

Which three functions give the typical, smallest and biggest number of a list?

A1: 70
A2: 80
A3: 90
A4: 60
B1: =AVERAGE(A1:A4)
B2: =MIN(A1:A4)
B3: =MAX(A1:A4)
column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
AVERAGE gives the mean, MIN the lowest and MAX the highest value.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
एवरेज = औसत, MIN = सबसे छोटा, MAX = सबसे बड़ा

CODE:
A1: 70
A2: 80
A3: 90
A4: 60
B1: =AVERAGE(A1:A4)
B2: =MIN(A1:A4)
B3: =MAX(A1:A4)

OUTPUT:
B1 shows 75, B2 shows 60, B3 shows 90

EXPLANATION:
AVERAGE adds the numbers and divides by how many numbers there are: (70+80+90+60)/4 = 75. MIN finds the lowest, which is 60, and MAX finds the highest, which is 90. All three ignore text and empty cells in a range.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
AVERAGE sab jodkar number ginti se bhaag deta hai. MIN sabse chhota aur MAX sabse bada number batata hai. Khali ya text cell ginti me nahi aate.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like checking a class: the shortest student, the tallest student and the typical height of all students.

SYNTAX PATTERN:
=AVERAGE(range) | =MIN(range) | =MAX(range)

ANATOMY:
AVERAGE, MIN, MAX = function names | range = cells to look at | brackets = hold the range

EXAMPLE 1:
A1: 70
A2: 80
A3: 90
A4: 60
B1: =AVERAGE(A1:A4) (shows 75, the mean)

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: 70
A2: 80
A3: 90
B1: =MAX(A1:A3,100) (shows 100, a typed number joins the range)

EXAMPLE 3:
A1: -5
A2: 3
A3: 0
B1: =MIN(A1:A3) (shows -5, negatives count too)

VARIATION:
=AVERAGE(A1:A4) skips blank cells but counts zero
=LARGE(A1:A4,2) gives the second biggest number
Status bar at the bottom shows Average, Count and Sum for selected cells

USED WITH:
SUM, COUNT, IF, LARGE, SMALL

RELATED CONCEPTS:
MEDIAN, LARGE, SMALL, COUNT

ALTERNATIVES:
MEDIAN, LARGE and SMALL, PivotTable summaries

FAMILY / GROUP:
AVERAGE, AVERAGEIF, MIN, MAX, MEDIAN, LARGE

WHERE IT IS USED:
Class marks analysis | Price comparison | Sales performance reports

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: My class average looks too low, why? | B: Check whether absent students were typed as 0, because zero is counted but blank is not.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ AVERAGE ignores zero values like blanks → ✓ AVERAGE counts a typed 0 as a number, but skips empty cells

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
AVERAGE vs MEDIAN: AVERAGE is the sum divided by the count, MEDIAN is the middle value when sorted.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not type 0 for missing marks if the average must skip them; leave the cell blank.

WRONG CODE:
A1: 70
A2: 80
A3: 90
B1: =AVG(A1:A3)

RIGHT CODE:
A1: 70
A2: 80
A3: 90
B1: =AVERAGE(A1:A3)

MEMORY TRICK:
MIN is little, MAX is big, AVERAGE is the middle ground.

REAL LIFE: PROJECT / WORK:
A teacher finds the highest, lowest and average score of a class test in three cells.

REAL LIFE: INTERVIEW / EXAM:
Interview question: What is the difference between AVERAGE and MEDIAN, and how does a zero affect AVERAGE?

REAL LIFE: DAILY LIFE:
It is like checking the cheapest, costliest and usual price of tomatoes in the market.

column1:
COUNT, COUNTA and COUNTBLANK

Which functions count only numbers, count every filled cell, or count the empty ones?

A1: 10
A2: Asha
A3: (empty)
A4: 25
B1: =COUNT(A1:A4)
B2: =COUNTA(A1:A4)
B3: =COUNTBLANK(A1:A4)
column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
COUNT counts numbers, COUNTA counts any filled cell and COUNTBLANK counts empty cells.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:

ROUND = पास की पूर्ण संख्या पर, ROUNDUP = हमेशा ऊपर, ROUNDDOWN = हमेशा नीचे

A1: 7.456

B2: =ROUNDUP(A1,2)
B3: =ROUNDDOWN(A1,2)

OUTPUT:
B1 shows 7.46, B2 shows 7.46, B3 shows 7.45

EXPLANATION:
ROUND looks at the next digit, 6, and rounds up to 7.46. ROUNDUP always moves away from zero, so it also gives 7.46. ROUNDDOWN always cuts toward zero, so it gives 7.45. The second number is how many decimal places to keep.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
ROUND paas wali value par le jata hai. ROUNDUP hamesha upar le jata hai aur ROUNDDOWN hamesha neeche. Doosra number batata hai kitne decimal rakhne hain.

B1: =ROUND(A1,0) (shows 3, a half rounds away from zero)

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: 1234
B1: =ROUND(A1,-2) (shows 1200, a negative digits value rounds to hundreds)

EXAMPLE 3:
A1: 9.99
B1: =ROUNDDOWN(A1,0) (shows 9, the decimals are cut off)

VARIATION:

=ROUNDDOWN(-3.7,0) gives -3 because it moves toward zero
=INT(7.9) gives 7 and always goes to the lower whole number

USED WITH:

RELATED CONCEPTS:
INT, TRUNC, CEILING, FLOOR

ALTERNATIVES:

FAMILY / GROUP:
ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, INT, TRUNC, MROUND

WHERE IT IS USED:

✗ Formatting a cell to 2 decimals also rounds the stored number → ✓ Format only changes how it looks; ROUND changes the stored value

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
ROUNDDOWN vs INT: for negative numbers ROUNDDOWN moves toward zero, while INT moves to the lower whole number.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not rely on cell formatting when the rounded value must be used in later formulas.

ROUND is Regular, UP is Upwards always, DOWN is Down always.

Which function lets Excel choose between two results depending on whether a test is true or false?

column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
IF checks a condition and returns one result if it is true and another if it is false.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
शर्त जाँचकर दो में से एक परिणाम देना

CODE:
A1: 55
B1: =IF(A1>=40,"Pass","Fail")

OUTPUT:
Pass

EXPLANATION:
IF takes three parts: a test, the result if the test is true, and the result if the test is false. Here 55 is greater than or equal to 40, so Excel returns Pass. Text results must be inside double quotes.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
IF function pehle condition check karta hai. Condition sahi hai to pehla jawab deta hai, galat hai to doosra. Text ko double quotes me likhna zaroori hai.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like a lift that goes up if you press up and goes down if you press down.

SYNTAX PATTERN:
=IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false)

ANATOMY:
logical_test = the question that is TRUE or FALSE | value_if_true = result when true | value_if_false = result when false | , = separates the parts

EXAMPLE 1:
Text result: A1: 55
B1: =IF(A1>=40,"Pass","Fail")
Shows: Pass

EXAMPLE 2:
Number result (discount): A1: 1200
B1: =IF(A1>=1000,A1*0.1,0)
Shows: 120

EXAMPLE 3:
Check for blank: A1 is empty
B1: =IF(A1="","Empty","Filled")
Shows: Empty

VARIATION:
=IF(A1>=80,"A",IF(A1>=40,"B","C")) (nested IF: A1 = 55 gives B)
=IF(A1>=40,"Pass") (if false it shows FALSE)
=IF(A1<>"","Done","") (blank when not done)

USED WITH:
AND, OR, SUM, COUNTIF

RELATED CONCEPTS:
AND, OR, IFS, IFERROR

ALTERNATIVES:
IFS function (Excel 2019 or later), SWITCH function, Conditional Formatting for colours

FAMILY / GROUP:
IF, IFS, IFERROR, AND, OR, NOT

WHERE IT IS USED:
Pass or Fail results in a marksheet | Discounts for bills above a limit | Showing Paid or Due on a fee list

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: I want a column that says Pass when marks are 40 or more, and Fail otherwise. | B: Use =IF(A1>=40,"Pass","Fail") and copy it down the column.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ IF(A1>=40,Pass,Fail) works without quotes around text → ✓ Without quotes Excel treats Pass as a name and shows #NAME?; write "Pass" and "Fail"

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
IF vs IFS: IF checks one test with two results, while IFS (newer versions) checks many tests in order without nesting.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not nest many IFs inside each other when a simple lookup would be clearer.

WRONG CODE:
=IF(A1>=40,Pass,Fail)

RIGHT CODE:
=IF(A1>=40,"Pass","Fail")

MEMORY TRICK:
IF = Test, Then this, Else that.

column1:
AND and OR

Which two functions let one test check several conditions, where one demands that all pass and the other only that any pass?

A1: 50
B1: 30
C1: =AND(A1>=40,B1>=40)
D1: =OR(A1>=40,B1>=40)
column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
AND returns TRUE only if all conditions are true; OR returns TRUE if at least one condition is true.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
AND में सारी शर्तें सही हों, OR में कोई एक सही हो

CODE:
A1: 50
B1: 30
C1: =AND(A1>=40,B1>=40)
D1: =OR(A1>=40,B1>=40)

OUTPUT:
C1 shows FALSE and D1 shows TRUE

EXPLANATION:
AND checks every condition, and since B1 (30) is below 40 it gives FALSE. OR needs only one true condition, and A1 (50) is at least 40, so it gives TRUE. Both return TRUE or FALSE, which you can place inside IF.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
AND me saari conditions sahi honi chahiye, warna FALSE. OR me koi ek condition sahi ho to TRUE. Dono TRUE ya FALSE dete hain.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
AND is like needing both a key and a password to open a locker; OR is like opening it with either the key or the spare card.

SYNTAX PATTERN:
=AND(test1, test2, ...) and =OR(test1, test2, ...)

ANATOMY:
AND = all must be true | OR = any one true is enough | test1, test2 = comparisons such as A1>=40 | Result = TRUE or FALSE

EXAMPLE 1:
AND result: A1: 50, B1: 30
C1: =AND(A1>=40,B1>=40)
Shows: FALSE

EXAMPLE 2:
OR result: A1: 50, B1: 30
C1: =OR(A1>=40,B1>=40)
Shows: TRUE

EXAMPLE 3:
Inside IF: A1: 50, B1: 30
C1: =IF(AND(A1>=40,B1>=40),"Pass","Fail")
Shows: Fail

VARIATION:
=AND(A1>=40,B1>=40,C1>=40) (three conditions: all must be true)
=OR(A1="Yes",B1="Yes") (any one Yes gives TRUE)
=NOT(A1>=40) (reverses TRUE and FALSE)

USED WITH:
IF, COUNTIFS, Conditional Formatting, NOT

RELATED CONCEPTS:
IF, NOT, XOR, IFS

ALTERNATIVES:
Nested IF formulas, multiplying and adding test results (advanced), COUNTIFS for counting

FAMILY / GROUP:
AND, OR, NOT, XOR, IF

WHERE IT IS USED:
Pass only if two subjects are passed | Discount if customer is new or bill is large | Alert when stock is low and not ordered

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: A scholarship is for students with marks 80 or more, or attendance 90 or more. | B: Then use =OR(A1>=80,B1>=90) because only one of the two needs to be true.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ AND and OR work the same way, just with different names → ✓ AND needs every condition true, while OR needs only one true condition

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
AND vs OR: AND is strict and needs all conditions to pass, while OR is relaxed and needs any one to pass.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not write =A1>=40 AND B1>=40 as in plain English; Excel needs the AND function with brackets and commas.

WRONG CODE:
=IF(A1>=40 AND B1>=40,"Pass","Fail")

RIGHT CODE:
=IF(AND(A1>=40,B1>=40),"Pass","Fail")

MEMORY TRICK:
AND = All needed; OR = One is enough.

An HR sheet marks an employee Eligible if experience is 2 years or more and performance rating is at least 3.

column1:
IFS and nested IF

How do you make Excel pick one result out of three or more, depending on a number such as marks?

A1: 72
B1: =IFS(A1>=90,"A",A1>=75,"B",A1>=60,"C",TRUE,"F")
column2:
MEANING (SHORT):
IFS checks several conditions in order and returns the result of the first one that is true.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
कई शर्तों को क्रम से जाँचकर पहली सही शर्त का परिणाम देना

CODE:
A1: 72
B1: =IFS(A1>=90,"A",A1>=75,"B",A1>=60,"C",TRUE,"F")

OUTPUT:
C

EXPLANATION:
Excel tests A1>=90 first, then A1>=75, then A1>=60. 72 fails the first two and passes the third, so the answer is C. The last pair TRUE,"F" works as an else, so a score below 60 gives F.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
Excel checks your conditions one by one from left to right. The first one that is true gives the answer and Excel stops there. So put the biggest limit first.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like a railway ticket check: the first rule that fits your ticket class decides your coach, and the later rules are never read.

SYNTAX PATTERN:
=IFS(condition1, result1, condition2, result2, ..., TRUE, default_result)
=IF(condition, result_if_true, IF(condition2, result2, result_if_all_false))

ANATOMY:
condition = a test that is TRUE or FALSE | result = what to show when that test is TRUE | TRUE as last condition = catch-all for everything else

EXAMPLE 1:
A1: 55
B1: =IF(A1>=90,"A",IF(A1>=60,"B","C"))

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: 15
B1: =IFS(A1<13,"Child",A1<20,"Teen",TRUE,"Adult")

EXAMPLE 3:
A1: 50
B1: =IFS(A1>=90,"A",A1>=60,"B")

VARIATION:
=IFS(A1>=90,"A",A1>=60,"B",TRUE,"C") - with a TRUE catch-all, no error
=IFS(A1>=90,"A",A1>=60,"B") - gives #N/A when A1 is 50, because no condition is true
=IF(A1>=60,"Pass","Fail") - plain IF for two outcomes only

USED WITH:
AND, OR, IFERROR, VLOOKUP

RELATED CONCEPTS:
IF, AND, OR, SWITCH

ALTERNATIVES:
Nested IF, SWITCH, VLOOKUP with approximate match, XLOOKUP with match mode

FAMILY / GROUP:
IF, IFS, IFERROR, IFNA, AND, OR, NOT

WHERE IT IS USED:
Grading marks into A, B, C | Sales commission slabs | Age or price groups

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: My grade formula gives C for a score of 95, why? | B: Check your order, put the score of 90 or more first, because Excel stops at the first true condition.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ Excel checks all the conditions and picks the best one → ✓ Excel stops at the first TRUE condition, so the order of conditions changes the answer

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
IFS vs nested IF: both do the same job, but IFS is easier to read and needs Excel 2019 or Microsoft 365, while nested IF works in every version.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not build nested IFs more than three or four levels deep, because they become very hard to read and fix.

WRONG CODE:
A1: 95
B1: =IFS(A1>=60,"C",A1>=75,"B",A1>=90,"A",TRUE,"F")

RIGHT CODE:
A1: 95
B1: =IFS(A1>=90,"A",A1>=75,"B",A1>=60,"C",TRUE,"F")

MEMORY TRICK:
Biggest first, TRUE last: big limits go in front, catch-all goes at the back.

A school office uses IFS on a marks sheet to turn every student's score into a grade in one column.

MEANING (SHORT):
COUNTIF counts the cells that meet one condition, and SUMIF adds the numbers that meet one condition.

एक शर्त पूरी करने वाले सेल गिनना या उनका जोड़ निकालना

A4: Goa

B3: 150
B4: 50
B5: 300

D2: =SUMIF(A1:A5,"Delhi",B1:B5)

OUTPUT:
D1 shows 3
D2 shows 550

EXPLANATION:
COUNTIF looks at A1:A5 and counts the cells equal to Delhi, which is 3. SUMIF checks the same range for Delhi and adds the matching numbers in B1:B5, which are 100, 150 and 300, giving 550.

B2: =EDATE(A2,1)

B4: =NETWORKDAYS(DATE(2024,3,4),DATE(2024,3,10))

MEANING (SHORT):
These four functions measure the gap between dates, move dates by months, find month ends, and count working days.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
तारीखों का अंतर निकालना, महीने आगे-पीछे करना, महीने का आखिरी दिन और कार्य दिवस गिनना

CODE:
A1: =DATE(2000,1,15)
A2: =DATE(2024,3,10)
B1: =DATEDIF(A1,A2,"Y")
B2: =EDATE(A2,1)
B3: =EOMONTH(A2,0)
B4: =NETWORKDAYS(DATE(2024,3,4),DATE(2024,3,10))

OUTPUT:
B1 shows 24
B2 shows 10-04-2024 (format dd-mm-yyyy)
B3 shows 31-03-2024
B4 shows 5

EXPLANATION:
DATEDIF counts complete years ("Y"), months ("M") or days ("D") between a start and an end date. EDATE moves a date by whole months, and EOMONTH returns the last day of a month that many months away. NETWORKDAYS counts Monday to Friday between two dates, including both ends.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
DATEDIF poore saal, mahine ya din batata hai. EDATE date ko mahine se aage ya peeche karta hai. EOMONTH mahine ka aakhri din deta hai, aur NETWORKDAYS Saturday Sunday chhod kar kaam ke din ginta hai.

SYNTAX PATTERN:

ANATOMY:
unit = "Y" years, "M" months or "D" days | months = how many months to move, negative goes back | holidays = optional list of dates to skip

EXAMPLE 1:
A1: =DATE(2000,1,15)
A2: =DATE(2024,3,10)
B1: =DATEDIF(A1,A2,"M")

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: =DATE(2024,1,31)
B1: =EDATE(A1,1)

EXAMPLE 3:
A1: =DATE(2024,3,4)
A2: =DATE(2024,3,10)
A3: =DATE(2024,3,6)
B1: =NETWORKDAYS(A1,A2,A3)

VARIATION:
=EOMONTH(DATE(2024,2,10),0) shows 29-02-2024
=EOMONTH(DATE(2024,2,10),1) shows 31-03-2024
=EDATE(DATE(2024,3,10),-2) shows 10-01-2024

USED WITH:
DATE, TODAY, IF, TEXT

RELATED CONCEPTS:
TODAY, DATE, WORKDAY, YEARFRAC

ALTERNATIVES:
YEARFRAC, WORKDAY, simple subtraction like =A2-A1 for days

FAMILY / GROUP:
DATEDIF, EDATE, EOMONTH, NETWORKDAYS, WORKDAY, YEARFRAC

Age and service years | EMI and fee due dates | Project working days

MINI CONVERSATION:

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ NETWORKDAYS skips the start date and the end date → ✓ NETWORKDAYS counts both the start date and the end date if they are working days

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
NETWORKDAYS vs WORKDAY: NETWORKDAYS counts working days between two dates, while WORKDAY gives the date after a number of working days.

RIGHT CODE:

A2: =DATE(2024,3,10)

DATEDIF = Difference, EDATE = Extra months, EOMONTH = End Of MONTH, NETWORKDAYS = Net work days.

MEANING (SHORT):
FILTER picks rows that meet a rule, UNIQUE removes repeats, and SORT puts items in order, and the results spill into the cells below.

MEANING IN LEARNER'S LANGUAGE:
एक फ़ॉर्मूला से पूरी सूची निकालना जो नीचे के सेल में अपने आप भर जाती है

CODE:
A1: Pune
A2: Agra
A3: Pune
A4: Delhi
A5: Agra
B1: =SORT(UNIQUE(A1:A5))

OUTPUT:
B1 shows Agra, B2 shows Delhi, B3 shows Pune

EXPLANATION:
UNIQUE removes the repeated cities and keeps each city once. SORT then puts them in A to Z order. Because this is one formula in B1, the three answers spill into B1, B2 and B3 by themselves.

SIMPLE EXPLANATION (HINGLISH):
Ek formula likho aur uska result neeche ke cells me khud fail jata hai. UNIQUE repeat hata deta hai, SORT sajata hai, aur FILTER sirf wahi rows deta hai jo shart puri karti hain. Ye Microsoft 365 ya Excel 2021 me milta hai.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like a sieve and a sorting tray: the sieve keeps only the wanted items, the tray removes repeats and arranges them.

SYNTAX PATTERN:

ANATOMY:
array = the cells to work on | include = a test like B2:B5>=60 | if_empty = text to show when nothing matches | sort_index = which column to sort by | sort_order = 1 for A to Z, -1 for Z to A

A2: Agra
A3: Pune
A4: Delhi
B1: =UNIQUE(A1:A4)

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: Asha
B1: 80
A2: Ravi
B2: 45
A3: Meena
B3: 90
A4: Tara
B4: 60
D1: =FILTER(A1:B4,B1:B4>=60)

EXAMPLE 3:
A1: Asha
B1: 80
A2: Ravi
B2: 45
A3: Meena
B3: 90
A4: Tara
B4: 60
D1: =SORT(A1:B4,2,-1)

VARIATION:

=SORT(A1:A4) sorts one column A to Z
=SUM(D1#) the # sign points to the whole spilled result

USED WITH:
SUM, COUNTA, XLOOKUP, Table (Ctrl+T)

RELATED CONCEPTS:
XLOOKUP, SORTBY, Table (Ctrl+T), Power Query

ALTERNATIVES:
The Filter button (Ctrl+Shift+L), Remove Duplicates on the Data tab, PivotTable

FAMILY / GROUP:
FILTER, UNIQUE, SORT, SORTBY, SEQUENCE, XLOOKUP

WHERE IT IS USED:
A live list of students who passed | A list of each city only once | A ranked leaderboard

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ I must copy the FILTER formula down to fill the list → ✓ You write it once in the first cell and the result spills down by itself

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
FILTER function vs Filter button: The Filter button hides rows in the same place, while the FILTER function writes a new list in other cells and the original data stays unchanged.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not put data in the cells below a spilling formula, because it will block the result with a #SPILL! error.

B1: 80
A2: Ravi
B2: 45
D1: =FILTER(A1:B2,B1:B2>=60)
E1: typed text blocks the spill (D1 shows #SPILL!)

RIGHT CODE:
A1: Asha
B1: 80
A2: Ravi
B2: 45
D1: =FILTER(A1:B2,B1:B2>=60)
E1: clear it so that the spill area D1:E1 is empty

MEMORY TRICK:
FILTER keeps, UNIQUE de-duplicates, SORT arranges, and one formula spills.

Power Query me aap ek baar saaf karne ke steps banate ho, aur Excel unhe yaad rakhta hai. Agli baar naya data aaye to Refresh All dabao aur wahi saare steps dobara chal jate hain.

REAL-LIFE ANALOGY:
Like a recipe card: you write the steps once and can cook the same dish again with new ingredients.

SYNTAX PATTERN:
Data tab > Get Data (or From Table/Range, or From Text/CSV) > Power Query Editor > Close & Load

ANATOMY:
Source = where the data comes from | Applied Steps = the list of recorded actions | Transform = clean-up actions like Remove Duplicates | Close & Load = write the result to a sheet | Refresh All = run all steps again

EXAMPLE 1:
Data tab > Get Data > From File > From Text/CSV > choose a CSV file > Load
Result: the CSV rows appear in a new sheet as a table

EXAMPLE 2:
A1: Name
A2: Asha
A3: Ravi
A4: Asha
Click a cell > Data > From Table/Range > select Name column > Remove Rows > Remove Duplicates > Close & Load
Result: Asha and Ravi, one time each

EXAMPLE 3:
Data tab > Get Data > Combine Queries > Append > choose two tables > OK > Close & Load
Result: the rows of the second table are added below the first table in one list

VARIATION:
Data tab > Refresh All (Ctrl+Alt+F5) runs every query again
Home tab > Merge Queries joins two tables like a lookup
Click the cross next to a step in Applied Steps to delete that step

USED WITH:
Table (Ctrl+T), PivotTable, CSV files, Refresh All

RELATED CONCEPTS:
PivotTable, Text to Columns, Table (Ctrl+T)

ALTERNATIVES:
Manual clean-up, Text to Columns, Remove Duplicates on the Data tab, VBA macros

FAMILY / GROUP:
Power Query, Get & Transform, Applied Steps, Query, Refresh All, M language

WHERE IT IS USED:
Monthly CSV imports | Combining many files into one table | Cleaning exported data before a PivotTable

MINI CONVERSATION:
A: Every month I get a new export and clean the same columns by hand. | B: Record the clean-up in Power Query once, and next month just click Refresh All.

COMMON MISTAKE:
✗ Power Query changes my original data table → ✓ It reads the source and writes a new result table, so the original data stays as it was

COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH:
Power Query vs a macro: Power Query records data-cleaning steps that refresh with new data, while a macro (VBA) records any clicks and keystrokes in Excel as code.

AVOID / DON'T:
Do not edit the loaded result table by hand, because the next refresh will overwrite your changes.

WRONG CODE:
Clean the new month's file by hand again, and then paste it over the old data every time

RIGHT CODE:
Load the file with Data > From Text/CSV, clean it in Power Query once, then use Data > Refresh All each month

MEMORY TRICK:
Power Query = record the clean-up once, replay it forever.

REAL LIFE: PROJECT / WORK:
An accountant loads a bank CSV every month, removes blank rows, changes the date type and refreshes the same query.

REAL LIFE: INTERVIEW / EXAM:
Interview: How would you combine twelve monthly files with the same columns into one table in Excel?

REAL LIFE: DAILY LIFE:
It is like a washing machine program: you choose the steps once and press start every week.
